problem:
Find the general solution of the differential equation

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{y{e}^{xy}-5}{\,4y-x{e}^{xy}\,},
$$

with the initial condition $y(0)=4.$

feedback.problem:
Find the general solution of the differential equation

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+5}{\,4y-x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\,},
$$

with the initial condition $y(0)=-2.$
feedback.worked_solution:
We start by rewriting this equation in differential form.

$$
P(x,y)\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\text{d}y=0
$$

Starting from 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+5}{4y-x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)},\end{aligned}
$$

we first multiply through by $(4y-x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy))\,\text{d}x$:

$$
(4y-x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy))\,\text{d}y=(y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+5)\,\text{d}x
$$

Then, we rearrange the terms:

$$
(y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+5)\,\text{d}x+(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-4y)\,\text{d}y=0
$$

Now, we should check for exactness. A differential equation of the form

$$
P(x,y)\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\text{d}y=0
$$

is exact if it passes the exactness test, i.e.,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}.
$$

For our differential equation, we have

$$
P(x,y)=y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+5,\,Q(x,y)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-4y.
$$

Now, let's compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+5) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-xy\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-4y) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-xy\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\end{aligned}
$$

So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}.\,✓
$$

Thus, our equation is exact.

Since the equation is exact, our solution $u(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂u}{∂x}=P(x,y),\,\frac{∂u}{∂y}=Q(x,y)
$$

First, we integrate $P(x,y)$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(x,y) & =\int P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+f(y) \\  & =\int (y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+5)\,\text{d}x+f(y) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+5x+f(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we integrate $Q(x,y)$ with respect to $y.$  Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(x,y) & =\int Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y+g(x) \\  & =\int (x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-4y)\,\text{d}y+g(x) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-2{y}^{2}+g(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing the two solutions, we see that we must have

$$
g(x)=5x,\,f(y)=-2{y}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution $u(x,y)=c$ is

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-2{y}^{2}+5x=c.
$$

The particular solution specified by the initial condition must have $y=-2$ when $x=0.$ These values determine the value of the constant $c.$ Substituting this into the equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-2{y}^{2}+5x & =c \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(0\cdot (-2))-2(-2)^{2}+5\cdot 0 & =c \\ c & =0-8 \\ c & =-8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-2{y}^{2}+5x=-8.
$$
